title: Slopes of Tangents and Instantaneous Rate of Change
overview: An average rate of change tells you what happened over an interval; an **instantaneous rate of change** tells you what is happening at a single moment — like the reading on a speedometer. Geometrically it is the slope of the **tangent** to the curve. In this section you will estimate instantaneous rates of change from graphs, tables and equations by using secants over smaller and smaller intervals.
objectives: Distinguish between average and instantaneous rates of change.
Estimate the slope of a tangent from a graph using a nearby secant or a sketched tangent.
Estimate an instantaneous rate of change from a table using nearby (preferably centred) points.
Estimate an instantaneous rate of change from an equation using very short intervals and the difference quotient.
Interpret instantaneous rates of change, including zero rates at local maximum and minimum points.

lessons.title: From average to instantaneous rate of change
lessons.body:
A car's trip computer may say your **average** speed was 72 km/h, but the **speedometer** shows how fast you are going *right now*. That "right now" rate is an **instantaneous rate of change**.

* An average rate of change describes an **interval** and is the slope of a **secant**.
* An instantaneous rate of change describes a single **point** and is the slope of the **tangent** line at that point.

A **tangent** to a curve at a point touches the curve at that point and has the same "direction" as the curve there.

```plot
title: Secants PQ getting closer to the tangent at P(2, 20) on d = 5t²
f: 5*x^2 | label=d = 5t²
f: 25*x - 30 | dashed; label=secant to Q(3, 45)
f: 20*x - 20 | label=tangent at P, slope 20
domain: 0, 4
range: -5, 60
points: (2,20), (3,45)
```

As the second point $Q$ slides towards $P$, the secant swings round and gets closer and closer to the tangent. The secant slopes **approach** the tangent slope.

lessons.title: Estimating from a graph
lessons.body:
Two graphical methods:

**Method 1 – a nearby secant.** Choose a point $Q$ on the curve close to $P$ and easy to read, then compute $m_{PQ} = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$.

**Method 2 – sketch the tangent.** Draw a line through $P$ that just touches the curve, choose a second point on *that line*, and compute its slope.

Parachutist example (distance $d$ in metres, time $t$ in seconds), at $P(2, 20)$:

* Secant to $Q(3, 45)$: $\dfrac{45 - 20}{3 - 2} = 25$ m/s.
* Tangent through $S(3, 40)$: $\dfrac{40 - 20}{3 - 2} = 20$ m/s.

Both are estimates. Accuracy depends on how well you read the coordinates and, for Method 2, how accurately you drew the tangent. The closer $Q$ is to $P$, the better the secant estimate.

lessons.title: Estimating from a table of values
lessons.body:
Use the tabulated points **closest to** the point of interest.

| $t$ (s) | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | 2.5 | 3.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $d$ (m) | 5 | 11.25 | 20 | 31.25 | 45 |

* Forward: $\dfrac{31.25 - 20}{2.5 - 2} = 22.5$ m/s.
* Backward: $\dfrac{20 - 11.25}{2 - 1.5} = 17.5$ m/s.
* **Centred** (using the points on both sides): $\dfrac{31.25 - 11.25}{2.5 - 1.5} = 20$ m/s.

For a smooth curve, the centred interval is usually the best estimate because the errors on the two sides partly cancel — it is also the average of the forward and backward estimates.

lessons.title: Estimating from an equation: shrinking the interval
lessons.body:
With an equation you can make the interval as small as you like. For $d(t) = 5t^2$ at $t = 2$:

| Interval | $\Delta d$ | $\Delta t$ | $\dfrac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $2 \le t \le 3$ | $45 - 20 = 25$ | 1 | 25 |
| $2 \le t \le 2.5$ | $31.25 - 20 = 11.25$ | 0.5 | 22.5 |
| $2 \le t \le 2.1$ | $22.05 - 20 = 2.05$ | 0.1 | 20.5 |
| $2 \le t \le 2.01$ | $20.2005 - 20 = 0.2005$ | 0.01 | 20.05 |
| $2 \le t \le 2.001$ | $0.020005$ | 0.001 | 20.005 |

The secant slopes approach **20**, so the velocity at 2 s is 20 m/s.

**General form.** The slope of the secant from $x = a$ to $x = a + h$ is the **difference quotient**

$$\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$

As $h$ gets very close to 0, this approaches the instantaneous rate of change at $x = a$.

> **Example.** For $f(x) = x^2$ at $x = 3$: $\dfrac{(3 + h)^2 - 9}{h} = \dfrac{6h + h^2}{h} = 6 + h$, which approaches **6** as $h \to 0$.

lessons.title: Interpreting instantaneous rates and turning points
lessons.body:
* A **positive** instantaneous rate of change means the function is increasing at that point (the tangent rises to the right).
* A **negative** value means it is decreasing there.
* A value of **zero** means the tangent is horizontal — this happens at **local maximum and minimum points**.

```plot
title: Tangent slopes on y = x³ − 3x
f: x^3 - 3*x | label=y = x³ − 3x
f: 2 | dashed; label=tangent at (−1, 2): slope 0
f: 9*x - 16 | dashed; label=tangent at (2, 2): slope 9
domain: -2.5, 3
range: -5, 8
points: (-1,2), (1,-2), (2,2)
```

If the instantaneous rate of change is negative at one point and positive at a later point, the graph must have turned around in between — a **local minimum** lies between them (and a local maximum if it goes from positive to negative).

Always include units: the instantaneous rate of change of distance (m) with respect to time (s) is a velocity in m/s.

keyTerms.definition: The rate of change at a single point; the slope of the tangent there.
A line that touches a curve at a point and matches the curve's direction at that point.
The point at which a tangent touches the curve.
$\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$, the slope of the secant from $x = a$ to $x = a+h$.

formulas.name: Difference quotient
formulas.meaning: Approaches the instantaneous rate of change at $x = a$ as $h$ gets close to 0.

formulas.name: Centred estimate
formulas.meaning: Uses points on both sides of $a$; usually a better estimate for small $h$.

steps: At $x = 2$ the function is decreasing; at $x = 4$ it is increasing.
To change from decreasing to increasing, the graph must turn: the tangent is horizontal (slope 0) somewhere between.
That point is a local minimum.
workedExamples.answer: There is a local minimum between $x = 2$ and $x = 4$.

misconceptions.myth: The instantaneous rate of change can be calculated exactly by plugging the same point in twice.
misconceptions.fact: With one point, $\Delta x = 0$ and the quotient is undefined; instead use very close points and see what the slopes approach.

misconceptions.myth: Any nearby secant gives the exact tangent slope.
misconceptions.fact: Secants only approximate; the approximation improves as the interval shrinks.
It shows instantaneous speed — the rate at that moment.

misconceptions.myth: A zero instantaneous rate means the function is zero.
misconceptions.fact: It means the tangent is horizontal (often a local max or min); the function value can be anything.

realWorld.title: Driving
realWorld.body: Speedometers and police radar measure instantaneous speed; trip computers report average speed.

realWorld.title: Medicine
realWorld.body: 'Five seconds after the spray, the bacteria population is decreasing at 60 bacteria per second' is an instantaneous rate of change.

realWorld.title: Environment
realWorld.body: Forest-fire crews track how fast a fire is spreading right now (ha/h) to decide where to send resources.

realWorld.title: Amusement rides
realWorld.body: Engineers check the steepness (instantaneous slope) of a roller-coaster track at every point to keep forces safe.

practice.question: Estimate the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x) = 3x^2$ at $x = 1$ using $h = 0.01$.
Classify each as average or instantaneous: (a) at 3 p.m. the plane was travelling at 850 km/h (b) the train averaged 130 km/h over the 10-h trip (c) he lost 4 kg per month over 5 months.
Use the difference quotient to find the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x) = x^2 - 2x$ at $x = 3$.
When are the instantaneous and average speeds the same?
practice.solution: When the speed is constant over the interval (distance–time graph is a straight line): every secant and tangent has the same slope.

practice.question: Why is a centred interval usually better than a one-sided interval for estimating from a table?
practice.solution: For a smoothly curving graph, a forward secant overestimates (or underestimates) and a backward secant does the opposite; using points on both sides balances these errors.

practice.question: The height of a ball is $h(t) = -4.9t^2 + 19.6t + 1$. Estimate its velocity at $t = 2$ s and interpret.
practice.solution: $\dfrac{h(2.001) - h(2)}{0.001} \approx -0.0049 \approx 0$ m/s. The ball is momentarily at rest — at its maximum height.

summary: The instantaneous rate of change at a point is the slope of the tangent at that point.
Estimate it from a graph (nearby secant or sketched tangent), from a table (closest points, preferably on both sides), or from an equation (very short intervals).
The difference quotient $\dfrac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$ approaches the instantaneous rate of change as $h$ approaches 0.
A zero instantaneous rate of change means a horizontal tangent, often at a local maximum or minimum.
Instantaneous rates have units and a sign that tells whether the function is increasing or decreasing at that moment.

questions.text: Estimate the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x) = {{a}}x^2$ at $x = {{p}}$ by computing the slopes of secants from $x = {{p}}$ to $x = {{p}} + h$ for $h = 0.1$, $0.01$ and $0.001$. Then state your estimate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Your estimate of the instantaneous rate of change

questions.text: The distance a parachutist has fallen is modelled by $d(t) = 5t^2$, where $d$ is in metres and $t$ in seconds. Estimate the parachutist's velocity at $t = {{t0}}$ s using an interval of 0.01 s. Explain why this is a velocity at an instant rather than an average.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimated velocity

questions.modelAnswer:
$d({{t0}}) = 5({{t0}})^2 = {{5*t0^2}}$ m and $d({{t0 + 0.01}}) = 5({{t0 + 0.01}})^2 = {{5*(t0+0.01)^2}}$ m.

$$\frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t} = \frac{ {{5*(t0+0.01)^2}} - {{5*t0^2}} }{0.01} = {{10*t0 + 0.05}} \text{ m/s}$$

So the velocity at {{t0}} s is about **{{10*t0}} m/s**. Strictly, 0.01 s is a very short interval, so this is an average over a tiny interval; as the interval shrinks the values approach {{10*t0}}, which is the instantaneous velocity (the slope of the tangent at $t = {{t0}}$).

rubric.point: Explains shrinking intervals approach tangent slope

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the velocity at $t = {{t0}}$ s using the next point in the table.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate it using the previous point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate it using the points on both sides, and explain which estimate is best.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Forward: $\dfrac{ {{4.9*(t0+0.5)^2}} - {{4.9*t0^2}} }{0.5} = {{9.8*t0 + 2.45:4}}$ m/s.

(b) Backward: $\dfrac{ {{4.9*t0^2}} - {{4.9*(t0-0.5)^2}} }{0.5} = {{9.8*t0 - 2.45:4}}$ m/s.

(c) Centred: $\dfrac{ {{4.9*(t0+0.5)^2}} - {{4.9*(t0-0.5)^2}} }{1} = {{9.8*t0:4}}$ m/s.

The centred estimate is the best: the curve bends upward, so the forward secant overestimates and the backward secant underestimates; using points on both sides of {{t0}} s balances the two errors. (It equals the average of the forward and backward estimates.)

questions.text:
The graph shows $f(x) = 0.5x^2$ and a tangent line at the point $P$.

```plot
f: 0.5*x^2
f: {{p}}*x - {{p^2/2}} | dashed
domain: -1, {{p+3}}
points: ({{p}},{{p^2/2}}), ({{p+2}},{{p^2/2+2*p}})
```

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the coordinates of the tangent point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the coordinates of another point on the tangent line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the slope of the tangent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: What does this slope represent?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The tangent point is $P({{p}}, {{p^2/2}})$.

(b) Another point on the tangent line is $({{p+2}}, {{p^2/2 + 2*p}})$.

(c) Slope $= \dfrac{ {{p^2/2 + 2*p}} - {{p^2/2}} }{ {{p+2}} - {{p}} } = \dfrac{ {{2*p}} }{2} = {{p}}$.

(d) This is the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $x = {{p}}$: at that point, $y$ is increasing at {{p}} units per unit of $x$.

rubric.point: Interprets as instantaneous rate of change

questions.text:
For each statement, decide whether it describes an average rate of change or an instantaneous rate of change. Give a reason.

(a) At 3 p.m., the plane was travelling at 850 km/h.
(b) The average speed of the train during the 10-h trip was 130 km/h.
(c) The fire was spreading at a rate of 2 ha/h.
(d) Five seconds after an antiseptic spray is applied, the bacteria population is decreasing at a rate of 60 bacteria per second.
(e) He lost 4 kg per month over a 5-month period.
(f) After being heated for 2 min, the water temperature was rising at 1°C/min.
questions.modelAnswer:
* (a) Instantaneous — a speed at one moment (3 p.m.).
* (b) Average — over a 10-h interval.
* (c) Instantaneous (as worded, the rate *right now*); it would be average if a time interval were given.
* (d) Instantaneous — at the moment $t = 5$ s.
* (e) Average — over a 5-month interval.
* (f) Instantaneous — at the moment $t = 2$ min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the instantaneous rate of change at $x = 2$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the instantaneous rate of change at $x = 4$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What special kind of point occurs between these two points? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
Use a short interval (e.g. $h = 0.001$) or, better, a centred interval.

(a) At $x = 2$: $\dfrac{f(2.001) - f(1.999)}{0.002} \approx -4.000$. The instantaneous rate of change is about $-4$ (decreasing).

(b) At $x = 4$: $\dfrac{f(4.001) - f(3.999)}{0.002} \approx 12.000$. About $12$ (increasing).

(c) The function changes from decreasing to increasing between $x = 2$ and $x = 4$, so the tangent must be horizontal somewhere in between: there is a **local minimum** point between $x = 2$ and $x = 4$ (in fact near $x \approx 2.87$).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the slope of the secant from $x = a$ to $x = a + h$ is $2a + h + {{b}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does this expression approach as $h$ gets very close to 0?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the instantaneous rate of change at $x = {{p}}$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $f(a + h) = (a + h)^2 + {{b}}(a + h) = a^2 + 2ah + h^2 + {{b}}a + {{b}}h$.

$f(a + h) - f(a) = 2ah + h^2 + {{b}}h$, so

$$\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h} = 2a + h + {{b}}.$$

(b) As $h$ approaches 0, the expression approaches $2a + {{b}}$.

(c) At $x = {{p}}$: $2({{p}}) + {{b}} = {{2*p + b}}$.

rubric.point: Simplifies the difference quotient to 2a + h + b

questions.text: For $f(x) = x^3 - {{3*m^2}}x$, estimate the instantaneous rate of change at $x = {{m}}$ and at $x = -{{m}}$ using centred intervals with $h = 0.001$. Explain the significance of your answers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Instantaneous rate of change at $x = {{m}}$

questions.modelAnswer:
$$\frac{f({{m}} + 0.001) - f({{m}} - 0.001)}{0.002} \approx 0.000 \qquad \frac{f(-{{m}} + 0.001) - f(-{{m}} - 0.001)}{0.002} \approx 0.000$$

(Exact values are $3({{m}})^2 - {{3*m^2}} = 0$.)

An instantaneous rate of change of 0 means the tangent is **horizontal**. These are the turning points: $f(-{{m}}) = {{2*m^3}}$ is a local maximum and $f({{m}}) = -{{2*m^3}}$ is a local minimum (the cubic rises, turns down at $x = -{{m}}$, and turns back up at $x = {{m}}$).

rubric.point: Interprets zero slope as horizontal tangent
Identifies local max and min with coordinates

questions.text: A section of roller coaster is modelled by $h(x) = 0.0025x(x - 8)(x - 16)(x - 32)$, $0 \le x \le 32$, where $x$ is horizontal distance and $h$ is height relative to the platform, in metres. Estimate the instantaneous rate of change (steepness) of the track at $x = {{x0}}$ m, and describe what it means.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Instantaneous rate of change

questions.text: A bacteria population is modelled by $P(t) = -2t^3 - 2t^2 + 3t + 800$, where $t$ is in minutes after a spray is applied. Estimate the rate at which the population is changing at $t = {{t0}}$ min, and interpret your answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rate of change at $t = {{t0}}$ min

questions.modelAnswer:
Centred interval, $h = 0.001$:
$$\frac{P({{t0}} + 0.001) - P({{t0}} - 0.001)}{0.002} \approx {{-6*t0^2 - 4*t0 + 3:4}}$$

At {{t0}} min, the population is **decreasing** at about {{abs(-6*t0^2 - 4*t0 + 3):4}} bacteria per minute.

questions.text: (a) Does a car's speedometer measure average speed or instantaneous speed? Explain. (b) Describe a situation in which the instantaneous speed and the average speed over an interval are the same, and explain why using the idea of secants and tangents.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A speedometer measures **instantaneous** speed — how fast the car is going at that moment.

(b) If a car travels at a constant speed (cruise control on a flat highway), the distance–time graph is a straight line. Every secant on a straight line *is* the line itself, and so is every tangent, so all slopes are equal: the instantaneous speed at any moment equals the average speed over any interval.

rubric.point: Explains with secant and tangent slopes on a straight line

questions.text: Water drains from a tank so that the volume, in litres, after $t$ minutes is $V(t) = {{C}}\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{40}\right)^2$. Estimate how fast the water is draining at $t = {{t0}}$ min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Instantaneous rate of change of the volume

questions.modelAnswer:
Centred interval, $h = 0.001$:
$$\frac{V({{t0}} + 0.001) - V({{t0}} - 0.001)}{0.002} \approx {{-C*(1 - t0/40)/20:4}} \text{ L/min}$$

The water is draining at about {{C*(1 - t0/40)/20:4}} L/min at $t = {{t0}}$ min (negative because the volume is decreasing).

questions.text:
The table shows the percent of Canadian households using the Internet for electronic banking (sample data).

| Year | 1999 | 2000 | 2001 | 2002 | 2003 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Households (%) | {{p1}} | {{p1 + d1}} | {{p1 + d1 + d2}} | {{p1 + d1 + d2 + d3}} | {{p1 + d1 + d2 + d3 + d4}} |

parts.label: a
parts.text: Average rate of change from 1999 to 2003

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the instantaneous rate of change in 2000 and in 2002. Give the 2002 estimate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare your answers to (a) and (b).

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\dfrac{ {{p1+d1+d2+d3+d4}} - {{p1}} }{4} = {{(d1+d2+d3+d4)/4:3}}$ percentage points per year.

(b) Using centred intervals: 2000: $\dfrac{ {{p1+d1+d2}} - {{p1}} }{2001 - 1999} = {{(d1+d2)/2:3}}$ per year. 2002: $\dfrac{ {{p1+d1+d2+d3+d4}} - {{p1+d1+d2}} }{2} = {{(d3+d4)/2:3}}$ per year.

(c) The average over 1999–2003 lies between the two instantaneous estimates: adoption was slower in 2000 and faster in 2002 than the four-year average suggests. The instantaneous estimates show the rate itself was increasing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Slope of the tangent

parts.label: b

questions.text: A ball is thrown upward with height $h(t) = -4.9t^2 + {{v}}t + 1$ (m) after $t$ seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the velocity at $t = 1$ s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the velocity is 0 at the highest point, and estimate when this happens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the maximum height.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Centred interval at $t = 1$: $\dfrac{h(1.001) - h(0.999)}{0.002} \approx {{v - 9.8:4}}$ m/s (upward).

(b) The velocity is 0 at the top. For any $t$, a centred estimate gives $v - 9.8t$ m/s; setting $ {{v}} - 9.8t = 0$ gives $t = \dfrac{ {{v}} }{9.8} \approx {{v/9.8:3}}$ s. (Check: estimates just before this time are positive, just after are negative.)

(c) Maximum height $h({{v/9.8:3}}) \approx {{-4.9*(v/9.8)^2 + v*(v/9.8) + 1:3}}$ m.

rubric.point: Explains velocity is zero at the top
Finds the time of maximum height

questions.text: Describe how you would estimate the instantaneous speed of a cyclist at exactly 10 s into a ride, given (a) a distance–time graph, (b) a table of distance readings every 0.5 s, and (c) an equation $d(t)$ for the distance. For each method, state one source of error and how to reduce it.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) **Graph:** draw the tangent at $t = 10$ s, choose a second point on the tangent, and compute its slope (or use a secant to a nearby point on the curve). Error: inaccurate tangent or misread coordinates — use a large, accurate graph and choose points far apart *on the tangent line*.

(b) **Table:** use the readings at 9.5 s and 10.5 s (a centred interval): $\dfrac{d(10.5) - d(9.5)}{1}$. Error: the interval is not infinitely small — use the closest readings, on both sides.

(c) **Equation:** compute $\dfrac{d(10 + h) - d(10)}{h}$ (or centred) for $h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001$ and see what value the results approach. Error: rounding in calculations — carry extra digits.

rubric.point: Table method with centred interval and error
Equation method with shrinking h and error

questions.text: Use the difference quotient to show that, for $f(x) = x^2$, the instantaneous rate of change at $x = a$ is $2a$. Then use your result to find the point on the graph where the tangent has slope {{2*m}}, and write the equation of that tangent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: $x$-coordinate of the point

parts.label: b
parts.text: $y$-intercept of the tangent

questions.modelAnswer:
$$\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h} = \frac{(a + h)^2 - a^2}{h} = \frac{2ah + h^2}{h} = 2a + h$$

As $h$ approaches 0, this approaches $2a$.

Slope {{2*m}}: $2a = {{2*m}} \Rightarrow a = {{m}}$, so the point is $({{m}}, {{m^2}})$.

Tangent: $y - {{m^2}} = {{2*m}}(x - {{m}})$, i.e. $y = {{2*m}}x - {{m^2}}$.
